terms.definition: The global network of interconnected computers that data travels across. The Web is just one of many services that run on top of it.
A system of linked documents (pages) accessed over the Internet via URLs and the HTTP protocol.
Uniform Resource Locator — the address of a specific resource on the web, made up of a scheme, domain, optional port, path, and optional query string.
Domain Name System — translates a human-readable domain name (like example.com) into the numeric IP address a browser needs to actually connect to a server.
HyperText Transfer Protocol — the protocol browsers and servers use to exchange requests and responses. HTTPS is HTTP encrypted with TLS/SSL for security.
The client (usually a browser) sends a request; the server processes it and sends back a response. Nearly all web communication follows this pattern.
A static site serves fixed files identical for every visitor. A dynamic site generates page content on the server per request, often from a database.
Document Object Model — the browser's live, in-memory tree representation of a page's HTML, which CSS and JavaScript both read and modify.

A single HTML building block, made of an opening tag, content, and a closing tag (e.g. a whole

The markup itself, like

or

— technically distinct from an 'element,' which is the tag plus its content, though the words are often used interchangeably.
Extra information added inside an opening tag, in the form name="value", such as href on a link or src on an image.

An element that never wraps content and has no closing tag, like ,
, or .

A block element starts on a new line and takes the full available width by default (like <div>). An inline element flows within a line of text and only takes up as much width as its content (like <span>).
Using elements that describe what content actually is (like <nav> or <article>) instead of generic containers (<div>/<span>) that carry no meaning.
Checking that markup follows the HTML specification correctly — properly nested and closed tags, required attributes present, etc.
Designing and building so people with visual, motor, auditory, or cognitive disabilities can perceive, understand, and use a page. "a11y" is a numeronym — a, 11 letters, y.
The four accessibility principles behind WCAG: content must be Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust.
Web Content Accessibility Guidelines — the W3C standard that most accessibility rules and legal requirements trace back to, with conformance levels A, AA, and AAA.

Accessible Rich Internet Applications — a set of attributes (role, aria-label, aria-live, etc.) that add accessibility information HTML can't express on its own. Best practice: don't use ARIA if a native HTML element already does the job.
A page region (like header, nav, main, footer) that assistive technology exposes for quick navigation — created automatically by using the right semantic element.
The text a screen reader announces for a control — computed from its label, aria-label, or visible text, in that general order of preference.
Focus is which element is currently active for keyboard input. Focus order is the sequence the Tab key moves through — it should follow the visual/logical reading order.
A link, usually the first thing in the page, that lets keyboard/screen-reader users jump straight past repeated navigation to the main content.
The alt attribute on an — a text description read by screen readers and shown if the image fails to load. Empty (alt="") marks an image as purely decorative.
A <form> element groups controls that get submitted together to a server, via the action and method attributes.
Connecting a <label> to its control, either via a matching for/id pair or by wrapping the control inside the label — required for accessibility and larger click targets.
The browser's built-in form validation (required, pattern, min/max, type checks, etc.) that runs with zero JavaScript.
<fieldset> groups related form controls; its required first child <legend> names the group — especially useful for radio/checkbox groups.
A <table> structured as genuinely tabular data — rows and columns of related values — as opposed to using a table purely to visually arrange page layout, which is discouraged.
An attribute on <th> (scope="col" or scope="row") that tells assistive technology exactly which cells that header describes.
Cascading Style Sheets — the language that controls how HTML content looks: color, spacing, layout, typography, and more.
The part of a CSS rule that determines which elements the rule applies to — e.g. a type selector (p), a class (.name), or an ID (#name).
The scoring system the browser uses to decide which of several conflicting CSS rules wins. Roughly: inline styles > IDs > classes/attributes/pseudo-classes > elements.
The overall algorithm that resolves which declaration applies when multiple rules could — based on specificity, source order, and importance (!important).
Some CSS properties (like color and font-family) pass down automatically from a parent element to its children unless overridden; others (like border) don't inherit by default.
Every element is a box made of content, padding, border, and margin, from the inside out — the foundation of how sizing and spacing work in CSS.
Controls whether an element's set width/height includes padding and border (border-box) or excludes them (content-box, the default).
A single CSS property that sets several related values at once, like margin (sets all four sides) or font (sets style, weight, size, line-height, and family together).
The visible area of a web page in the browser window (or on a device screen) — the basis for viewport units (vw/vh) and the viewport meta tag.
Building a page so its layout adapts to different screen sizes, using flexible units, media queries, and flexible layout systems like Flexbox and Grid.
A CSS rule block, like @media (min-width: 768px){...}, that only applies its styles when a condition about the viewport (or other device feature) is true.
The specific viewport width where a design's layout changes via a media query, e.g. switching from a stacked mobile layout to a multi-column desktop one.
Writing base CSS for small screens first, then using min-width media queries to add complexity as the screen grows — the opposite of desktop-first.
A one-dimensional CSS layout system (display: flex) for arranging items in a row or column, with powerful alignment and spacing controls.
A two-dimensional CSS layout system (display: grid) for arranging items across both rows and columns at once, ideal for whole-page layouts.
The position property (static, relative, absolute, fixed, sticky) that controls how an element is placed relative to normal flow, an ancestor, or the viewport.
Controls which of several overlapping positioned elements renders in front — higher numbers appear on top. Only affects elements with a position other than static.
A selector (single colon, like :hover or :nth-child()) that matches an element based on a state or position it's already in, without needing an extra class in the HTML.
A selector (double colon, like ::before or ::first-letter) that targets or inserts content into a sub-part of an element that has no node of its own in the HTML.
A selector that matches based on an HTML attribute's presence or value, like [type="email"] or [href^="https"].
A symbol connecting two selectors that describes a relationship between them — descendant (space), child (>), adjacent sibling (+), or general sibling (~).
A reusable value declared with two dashes (--name: value;) and read with var(--name) — unlike a preprocessor variable, it's live in the browser and can change at runtime.
A CSS function that lets you mix units in one expression, like calc(100% - 40px).
em is relative to the parent element's font-size (compounds when nested); rem is always relative to the root <html> font-size, making it more predictable.
Defines a named sequence of style states at percentage checkpoints (0% to 100%), used to drive a CSS animation.
A transition needs a trigger (like :hover) and moves once from state A to state B. An animation (via @keyframes) can run automatically and loop through many steps with no trigger.
A media feature that matches when a user has requested less motion at the OS level — respecting it by disabling/simplifying animations is an accessibility best practice.
JavaScript Object Notation — a lightweight, text-based data format (used throughout this site's own tutorial/quiz/reference content) that's easy for both humans and machines to read.
A browser storage API that saves small amounts of data on the user's own device, persisting between visits — this is how the site remembers your progress with no backend server.
Search Engine Optimization — structuring content so search engines can understand and rank it well, e.g. via a good <title>, meta description, and semantic HTML.
